title: What Is $1,000 From 1999 Worth in 2026 Dollars?
body:
$1,000 from 1999 has the same buying power as roughly $2,000 in 2026, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics Consumer Price Index. That average hides a split: the same money buys far more computer than it did in 1999 and far less house. The median existing home sold for $417,500 in September 2026, and the average employer family health premium reached $26,993 in 2025.

Quick facts
Status today
A 1999 dollar is worth about 50 cents of 2026 buying power
$1,000 in 1999
About $2,000 in 2026 dollars (BLS CPI)
Median household income, 1999
$41,994 (U.S. Census Bureau)
Family health premium
$26,993 a year in 2025, with workers paying $6,850 (KFF)
Median home price today
$417,500 in September 2026 (National Association of Realtors)

Why a thousand dollars felt like real money in 1999

In 1999, a thousand dollars was a meaningful slice of a household's year. The U.S. Census Bureau put median household income for 1999 at $41,994, so $1,000 was about 2.4 percent of what the household in the middle of the country earned across twelve months.

It was also the going price of the most expensive thing in most living rooms that was not furniture. The Register, citing the research firm PC Data, reported that the average US retail PC price had fallen 19 percent to $928 by May 1999, and that machines selling for under $1,000 had taken 71 percent of the retail market.

That is the anchor people remember. A thousand dollars was a computer: a tower, a monitor, a keyboard and a 56k modem that tied up the phone line. Gateway shipped it in a cow-spotted box, and a family expected the machine to last three or four years before it felt slow.

Everything below measures that same $1,000 against the things it used to cover, using price series that run from 1999 to now.

Is $1,000 still a lot of money in 2026?

Measured against the Consumer Price Index, it is worth half of what it was. $1,000 from 1999 has the same buying power as roughly $2,000 in 2026, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics CPI inflation calculator. Prices across the basket the BLS tracks have about doubled in 27 years.

Turn that around and a 2026 dollar buys about half of what a 1999 dollar bought. A thousand dollars sitting in a 2026 checking account is, in 1999 terms, about $500.

That is the headline number, and it is also the number that misleads people. The CPI is an average of a basket, and almost nothing in the basket actually doubled. Some categories tripled. Others fell by more than half. Which ones a household buys decides whether 27 years feels like a doubling or something a lot worse.

Three categories carry most of the gap: housing, health insurance and computers.

Why housing pulled away from the inflation average

Housing is the category that broke the average. The National Association of Realtors put the median price of an existing home at $417,500 in September 2026, up 1.3 percent from $412,300 a year earlier and the 39th consecutive month of year-over-year price increases.

General prices roughly doubled since 1999. Home prices did considerably more than that, and the monthly payment attached to them moved with mortgage rates on top of the price itself.

The market sitting on top of those prices has stalled rather than crashed. Sales ran at a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.99 million in September 2026, 2.2 percent below the same month in 2025, while unsold inventory reached 1.60 million homes, a 4.8-month supply. "Supply is not really an issue anymore," NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun said in October 2026. "So it's really the demand that is contracting."

What $1,000 does here has changed in kind rather than degree. In 1999 a thousand dollars was a real contribution to a down payment on a median-priced house. In 2026 it is a fraction of one month's carrying cost on one, which is why the same sum feels so much lighter even though the CPI says it only lost half its value.

Is health insurance where the purchasing power went?

For a lot of households, yes, though the recent numbers are more complicated than the long run. KFF has run the same employer health benefits survey every year since 1999, which makes it one of the steadiest price series in American life.

In 2025 the average annual premium for employer-sponsored family coverage was $26,993, up 6 percent in a year, with workers paying $6,850 of it out of their own paychecks. Single coverage averaged $9,325.

Set that against the thousand dollars. In 2025, $1,000 covered about two weeks of the average family premium. KFF also reports that family premiums rose about 26 percent over five years, roughly in line with inflation and wage growth across the same stretch, so most of the gap opened over decades rather than in the last few years.

KFF president and chief executive Drew Altman is not forecasting relief. "There is a quiet alarm bell going off," he said when the survey was published in October 2025, and added that "with GLP-1s, increases in hospital prices, tariffs, and other factors, we expect employer premiums to rise more sharply next year."

Why computers went the other way

Technology is the one large category that moved down instead of up. The PC Data figures from 1999 are the clearest marker: an average US retail price of $928 in May, already down 19 percent in a year, with sub-$1,000 machines taking 71 percent of the market. The cheap computer was becoming the normal computer.

In 2026 the same thousand dollars sits near the top of the mainstream laptop market rather than in the middle of it. The middle moved down underneath it, and the capability of an entry-level machine moved past anything sold in 1999.

Two forces did that, and neither shows up cleanly in a price index. Components got cheaper per unit of performance every year, and the software most people use moved into the browser, so the hardware stopped needing to be impressive to be enough.

The same arithmetic run across forty pieces of 90s hardware converted into 2026 dollars shows the pattern holding almost everywhere. The closer a product sits to a silicon chip, the worse it does at holding its price.

What the comparison gets wrong if you stop at the CPI

The doubling figure is correct and incomplete. It tells you what an average basket costs. It does not tell you that the basket itself changed shape.

A 1999 household paid separately for long-distance calls, a film camera, a camcorder, a CD collection, a road atlas, an encyclopedia and a Friday night video rental. One 2026 phone absorbed all of them. Those substitutions never register as savings, because a price index tracks the price of things rather than the disappearance of things.

The reverse is the part people feel. Housing and health insurance are not subject to any of that substitution. Neither can be downloaded, made smaller, or folded into a device already in a pocket, and both are exactly the categories that ran past the average.

So the short answer holds: $1,000 from 1999 is worth about $2,000 in 2026. The longer answer is that the same money now buys far more computer, far less house, and about two weeks of a family health premium that runs $26,993 a year.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is $1,000 from 1999 worth in 2026?

$1,000 from 1999 has about the same buying power as $2,000 in 2026, based on the Bureau of Labor Statistics Consumer Price Index. Prices roughly doubled over the 27 years from 1999 to 2026, so a 2026 dollar buys about half of what a 1999 dollar bought.

Did $1,000 really buy a computer in 1999?

Yes, and by 1999 it bought an above-average one. The Register, citing PC Data, reported an average US retail PC price of $928 in May 1999, down 19 percent in a year, with machines under $1,000 taking 71 percent of the retail market. That computer was usually the most expensive electronic item in the house.

What was the median household income in 1999?

Median household income in the United States was $41,994 in 1999, according to the U.S. Census Bureau's Census 2000 brief on household income. Converted with the Consumer Price Index, that is roughly $84,000 in 2026 dollars.
